text.tspan: Section 8.3: Hypothesis Testing Means
The t-distribution looks very similar to a normal distribution, but due to the uncertainty in the standard
deviation, it is a little flatter and a little wider. There is a slightly different distribution for every sample
size and associated
n
– 1 degree of freedom. The tails contain a little more area than the standard
normal, and the middle contains a little less area. As the sample size increases, the t-distribution will get
closer to normal (this is a result of the central limit theorem from section 7.3). That is why the sample
size is included in the computation of the t-statistic.
See figure 8.11
. Observe that the larger the sample
size is, the higher the degrees of freedom are, and the closer the t-distribution is to the standard normal
curve.
Figure 8.11
: Student’s t-distribution for 1, 2, and 10 degrees of freedom, and standard normal distribution.
Degrees of freedom are an odd concept. Why are the degrees of freedom
n
The degrees of freedom
count how many “independent” pieces of information there are in a sample if we already know the mean.
One might think that we need all
n
data points, but it turns out that we only need
n
It is the same
reason we divide by
n
– 1 when we compute the sample standard deviation (section 3.2). Think of this
example. If 4 students are offered a choice of 4 different donuts, say 1chocolate, 1 maple, 1 glazed, and
1sprinkled, then the first three students who pick have choices. But the last student has no freedom to
choose. Their choice is determined for them. They simply take whatever donut is left. So, there are 4 –
1 = 3 students who are free to choose, one less than the number in the group. The Degrees of freedom in
a t-distribution work in a similar way. And because the sample standard deviation is part of the
calculation of the t-statistic, it uses
n
– 1, just like the sample standard deviation.
STATBELT Utility- Probability for Student’s t-Distribution
To use STATBELT Utility to find probability from a t-distribution:
Select Calculators → T-distribution Calculator.
Type the degrees of freedom DF = n – 1.
Under “Find a probability,” choose the inequality you need and type the value or values of t. (The
calculator writes T for the variable.)
Choose “P(T < a)” or “P(T > a)” for one value.
Choose “P(a < T < b)” to calculate a probability between two values.
The probability and a graph appear as soon as you type. There is no button to click.
NOTE: The calculator gives the probability and shows the t-distribution with the probability shaded as
area. Click “Open graph in a new window” to see a larger graph.
